args.text: [lane-plover] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: if a site moves to a new server, users keep being sent to the old one, causing errors or outages. (2) Slow failover: when traffic must be redirected during a fault, the old answer lingers, so recovery takes longer. (3) Prolonged poisoning: if a false answer is cached, whether by attack or mistake, it stays in place and misleads users until it expires.

[lane-plover] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail unpredictably, so a client often cannot tell whether its first request succeeded, and it must be free to try again. If repeating a request has the same effect as sending it once, a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicated order.

[lane-plover] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (version 7 of the Universally Unique Identifier) as a primary key: (1) Because the leading part is a timestamp, new keys arrive roughly in order, which keeps database indexes tidy and inserts fast, but anyone who sees a key can read approximately when the row was created, which may leak information. (2) Each key takes 16 bytes, which is larger than a typical whole-number key, so indexes and related tables use more storage and memory, and keys are harder for people to read or type.

[lane-plover] A write-ahead log is a record that a database writes to disk before it changes the main data, describing each change it is about to make. If the system crashes part-way through, it can read the log on restart to finish or undo those changes, so no committed work is lost and the data is not left half-written.

[lane-plover] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: a newer client may change speed, retries or defaults, so unpinned runs could measure the client's changes rather than the system under test. (2) Repeatability: others, or you later, can rerun the same set-up and trust that any difference in results comes from the thing being tested.

[lane-plover] Backpressure is a way for a queue to push back on whoever is adding work when the queue is filling faster than it is being emptied. The sender is slowed, paused or told to try later, so the queue does not grow without limit and run out of memory or make everything wait ever longer.

[lane-plover] A cron job (a task run on a timetable) can run twice in two ways: (1) two machines carry the same schedule, for example after a server is copied or a standby is added; (2) a run lasts longer than the gap between runs, so the next one starts while the first is still going. One guard: take a lock before starting, so a second copy that cannot get the lock exits at once.

[lane-plover] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item in a replicated store (one that keeps copies of data on several machines). Instead of erasing the item outright, the store records that it was deleted, so a copy that missed the deletion does not bring the old item back. Tombstones are cleared away only after every copy has had time to learn of the deletion.

[lane-plover] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no change in between, so a plain rerun gives a different result; (2) its failures depend on timing, order or environment, such as running only when another test runs first, or only on a slow machine. A truly failing test fails every time until the code is fixed.

[lane-plover] A lease-based lock gives a machine the lock for a fixed span of time, after which it expires. Clock skew means machines disagree about the time. (1) If the holder's clock runs slow, it believes its lease is still valid after the lock service has expired it and handed it to another machine. (2) Then two machines both think they hold the lock, and they may write at the same time. A fencing token, a number that rises with each new lease, lets storage reject the older holder.
